A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same YRC-Bench research study. All 21 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable; their text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of coordination policies across 19 environments, including baseline comparisons, oracle diagnostics, and feature analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original coordination experiments across 19 environments and reports additional novice-to-expert score analyses and computational costs.

M1.justification: The weakened-novice validator and main policy components are retained. However, v2 Section 5 delegates when the score is at least the threshold, whereas v1 and v2 Appendix A.3 delegate below the threshold. This internal conflict prevents reliably identifying an actual inference-rule change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same three MiniGrid environments, eleven Procgen games, and five CLIPort tasks, retaining the same represented training and test scenarios. The added analyses use this existing coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the four rule-based strategies, five logit measures, Deep SVDD feature variants, and RLOracle variants. The headline change from 23 to 10 methods reflects grouping variants and treating RLOracle separately, rather than adding or removing comparators.

E3.justification: Deep SVDD threshold candidates change from linearly spaced score values in v1 Appendix A.6.2 to percentiles in v2 Appendix A.3.2. v2 also explicitly restricts the reward penalty to expert-controlled steps. These are reported protocol revisions; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds diagnostics quantifying novice-to-expert performance gaps and computational costs in Appendices D.5–D.6. The oracle-component analysis, feature comparisons, and near-oracle case studies already existed in v1 and are largely retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v2 introduces propagated uncertainties for novice-to-expert ratios and their suite averages in Equations 2–3 and Figure 12. The existing AUC bootstrap retains 1,000 simulations, 1,600 episode returns, and 256 samples per simulation; an increase in independent training runs is not established.

E6.justification: Deep SVDD scores change extensively in v1 Figure 12 versus v2 Figure 9, and normalized diagnostic results also change. v1 Section 6.2/Figure 6 reports logit superiority in 10 of 19 environments; v2 Appendix D.3/Figure 10 instead reports one logit win, two OOD wins, and sixteen ties. Novice-to-expert ratios and runtime results are newly reported. These are revised results, not established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 1 adds the expert-action indicator missing from v1 Equation 4 and derives the accumulated assistance penalty. v1 Equation 8's explicit requirement that the weakened novice achieve at most half the novice's training performance disappears. Neither version develops theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 narrows the novelty framing from introducing YRC and the additional ability to request control back to introducing the unsupervised YRC-0 variant of existing assistance problems. The benchmark, simulated validation approach, and principal claims about inconsistent method performance and restricted policy spaces remain.

C2.justification: The interpretation of logit versus OOD methods shifts from a fundamental logit advantage to largely tied performance. v2 additionally explains that validator reliability on restricted threshold policies may fail for richer policies because of overfitting. Conversely, it drops v1's explicit discussion of excluding environments with poorly matched simulated test conditions, changing the documented applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds suite-specific feature-extraction descriptions, implementation-source references, GPU and memory specifications, and detailed training/evaluation times. It substantially condenses the earlier framework and PPO documentation. These changes expand some reproducibility information while removing other details; they do not establish underlying implementation changes.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned around training supervision, active learning, and zero-shot coordination, with corresponding citation additions. The expert-behavior-understanding discussion is removed, as is Trinh et al. (2024), which v1 explicitly identified as a close precursor.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, problem exposition, and benchmark discussion are extensively rewritten. Evaluation material moves into the benchmark section, proposal and validation are grouped together, results become numbered findings, appendices are reorganized, and the standalone societal-impact section is removed.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. v2 adds an introductory illustration, uncertainty-measure and runtime tables, and novice-to-expert plots; expands the benchmark illustration; relocates several analyses and the bootstrap algorithm; and reduces four pseudocode displays to two. Existing comparison plots are also rearranged and recaptioned.

improvement.justification: v2 improves the assistance-cost formulation, adds useful feature-extraction documentation, and qualifies validator reliability for richer policies. However, its conflicting threshold directions obscure the inference procedure, and its new compute reporting states 1,347 GPU hours in Section 6 versus over 1,347 GPU days in Appendix D.6. Removal of the earlier environment-exclusion explanation also reduces transparency. These benefits and reliability problems prevent a confident net quality judgment.
